body:
It's banking on this patient investor and more operational freedom than its peers for the right IPO conditions down the line

Exactly a year ago, The Eye Foundation—a 40-year-old eye-care chain based in Coimbatore—raised external equity for the first time. Its choice of investor, though, was rather unusual.

Most of its competitors had gravitated towards healthcare-focused private-equity funds, such as Temasek, Blackstone, TPG, and KKR, which have collectively invested over $15.5 billion in healthcare in India over the last five years. Of this, 60% went to hospitals.

The Eye Foundation, on the other hand, chose the consumer-brands-and-retail VC fund Verlinvest, which has backed the likes of yogurt brand Epigamia, home-and-sleep-solutions company Wakefit, and beauty-and-personal-care platform Purplle.

In October 2025, Verlinvest invested Rs 650 crore for a 20% stake in The Eye Foundation.

The eye-care chain’s founder and CEO, D Ramamurthy, acknowledged that choosing an FMCG fund was “unusual for the sector”. “But we did not want a fly-by-night operator—somebody with a definite timeline who wants to exit in five years,” he said.

The chain had quite a few “suitors”, as Ramamurthy put it, courtesy of its robust balance sheet. But it chose Verlinvest because it offered “a very good valuation”, valuing the company at roughly the same level as competitor ASG Eye Hospital and above that implied by Dr Agarwal’s latest fundraise.

In FY27, Ramamurthy claims The Eye Foundation’s revenue is on track to jump by almost 90% year-on-year to touch Rs 550 crore. In the last few years, the company’s topline has grown steadily, touching Rs 278 crore in FY24, Rs 330 crore in FY25, and Rs 409 crore in FY26, he claimed. Its Ebitda margin, meanwhile, has hovered around 35%.

Margins above 30% are quite surprising in healthcare, particularly given the regulatory cloud hanging over the sector, according to two healthcare analysts The Ken spoke to.

For comparison, Dr Agarwal’s and ASG had margins of around 29% (FY26) and 22.6% (FY25), respectively.

On the whole, both chains seem to be contending with their PE investors. Dr Agarwal’s is backed by TPG and Temasek, who put in a combined Rs 1,050 crore in 2022 and Rs 640 crore in 2023—most of which has gone into acquisitions. In the three years to FY26, the company spent Rs 1,215 crore on acquisitions, even though it generated only about Rs 315 crore in free cash flow.
